office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The School Town of Highland is the public school district for the town of Highland in Lake County, with its administration center at 9145 Kennedy Ave. [24, 25]. This guide did not verify a current enrollment figure. In July 2026 the district reported a 98% graduation rate and a 97% IREAD passing rate [26].

The board has five members, all elected at large: President Patrick Krull, Vice President Robert Kuva, Secretary Erica Smith-Gomez, Victor A. Garcia and Richard Alyea [27, 28]. In 2022 voters filled three at-large seats, electing Garcia (3,931 votes), Smith-Gomez (3,782) and Kuva (3,584) over Carol Parker (2,820) and Richard (Rick) E Volbrecht Jr (2,491) [29]. In 2024 they filled two seats, electing Krull (4,099) and Rick Alyea (3,687) over Allencia Ballard (3,645) and Volbrecht (3,442) [30].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: the Lake County sample ballot says 'Vote for not more than Three (3)' in the School Town of Highland at-large race. The state list shows 'vote for 1' [31, 6]. The three seats are those won in 2022. All three incumbents, Garcia, Kuva and Smith-Gomez, are running again. The fourth candidate is Volbrecht, who ran unsuccessfully in 2022 and 2024 [31, 29, 30]. Krull and Alyea are not on this ballot [30]. On the ballot, Garcia and Smith-Gomez are listed as Independent, Volbrecht as Republican, and Kuva with no party [31].

Superintendent turnover (2026): on July 2, 2026 the board accepted the resignation of Dr. Brian Smith, superintendent for 13 years, and named Assistant Superintendent Dr. Ryan Erdelac interim superintendent [32, 26]. Erdelac resigned as assistant superintendent effective Aug. 20, 2026 [33]. On Aug. 18, 2026 the board voted to appoint Dr. John Schwuchow, a former elementary school teacher who said he was glad to be returning to Highland, as interim superintendent retroactive to Aug. 11 [33]. The board president said a new posting and a hearing were required before Schwuchow could be made permanent [33]. A public notice set a Sept. 14, 2026 hearing on a proposed three-year superintendent contract running from Sept. 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029. It lists a $193,500 salary and $242,159.97 in total annual compensation and benefits [34]. The district's staff directory now lists Schwuchow as superintendent [35].

August 2026 storm: after a severe storm on Aug. 11, 2026, the administration center lost power and the board postponed an Aug. 17 special meeting on the superintendent contract [36]. On Aug. 25 the board voted to keep paying eligible non-certified employees for their regular workdays from Aug. 11 to Aug. 21 [37]. The first day of school was Aug. 25 [38, 33].

Budget, property taxes and referendums: in May 2023 Highland voters rejected the district's operating referendum, 2,416 votes (52.25%) to 2,208 (47.75%) [39]. The district had said it was losing revenue to declining enrollment and changing demographics and had the lowest school tax rate in the area [40]. Members of the public raised a possible referendum at board meetings in January 2026 and raised the 2023 referendum's failure in August 2026 [28, 33]. In February 2026 Garcia reported meeting Highland's legislators about challenges the district expects from Senate Enrolled Act 1 [41]. On April 21, 2026 the board hired Policy Analytics to study property tax impacts and revenue [42]. On July 21, 2026 it approved transferring up to $528,581.51 from the Debt Service Fund to the Operations Fund in 2026 [25]. There is no Highland school question on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot [31].

Facilities and bonds: projects from the 2025 general obligation bond include high school and middle school gym bleachers and HVAC. In July 2026 the board hired The Skillman Corporation ($110,450) to manage that work and raised Schmidt Associates' architectural fee from $170,000 to $227,357 [25]. In September 2026 the board held hearings on a new bond for facility, athletic, safety and security improvements and for buses, equipment and technology [43]. Its notice of preliminary determination lists a maximum of $6,800,000 over five years and estimates no net increase in the debt service tax rate as existing debt matures [44].

Other 2025–2026 items: in July 2026 the board approved a high school handbook change putting in place the state's 'bell-to-bell' personal device ban (SEA 78) [25]. It also approved a $109,348.64 agreement with the Town of Highland for a school resource officer [25]. In February 2026 Smith-Gomez reported that state special education funding had been cut in every category for the year [41]. Members of the public raised the enrollment of out-of-district students at meetings in August 2025 and January 2026 [45, 28].

Forums: this guide found no candidate forums, questionnaires or news coverage of the 2026 Highland race. Three of the four candidates are sitting board members whose motions and votes appear in the board minutes cited here.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, first elected in 2022 and now board secretary. Listed as Independent [29, 28, 31].
background: Won an at-large seat in 2022 with 3,782 votes [29]. Elected board secretary in January 2026 [28].
Serves as Highland's representative on the board of the Northwest Indiana Special Education Cooperative (NISEC), which reelected her as its president in early 2026 [41].
path_to_ballot: Listed as Independent on the state list and the Lake County sample ballot [6, 31].

items: In board reports she said state special education funding was reduced in every category for the current year, and that 51 more students were in the severe category [41]. She has also reported on NISEC's costs, its 2027 draft budget and its search for a new director [46, 47].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member [27]. On Aug. 18, 2026 she made the motion to appoint Dr. John Schwuchow interim superintendent, which passed unanimously [33]. She seconded the July 2, 2026 motion accepting Dr. Brian Smith's resignation [32].
